tip: The -wch ending makes a command to chi, formal or group: Trowch means turn. Compare Eisteddwch, sit down, and Edrychwch, look.
well is the irregular comparative of da, good. na means than: heddiw'n well na ddoe, today is better than yesterday.
Add -ach to an adjective for the comparative: oer, cold, becomes oerach, colder. na after it means than.
fy, my, triggers nasal mutation: taid, grandfather, becomes fy nhaid. The t turns to nh.
Welsh builds tens as a unit plus deg, ten: dri deg is thirty, literally three tens.
Use am for clock times: am chwech means at six. am can also mean for or about.
Placing yn before an adjective makes it adverbial: cyflym, fast, softens to gyflym, meaning fast or quickly.
Give age with oed after a number: yn ddeg oed is ten years old, literally ten age.
ers marks how long something has held true: ers ugain mlynedd, for twenty years. It pairs with the present tense.
Feminine ei, her, is often echoed by hi after the noun: ei llais hi, her voice, which removes any his or her ambiguity.
Bydda i is I will: Bydda i'n ymarfer means I will practise. Keep yn before the verb, as in the present.
Masculine ei, his, soft-mutates the next word: teulu, family, becomes ei deulu, his family.
Welsh has no verb to have. Use gyda, with: does dim amser gyda ni means we have no time, literally no time with us.
mor before an adjective, plus a or ag before a vowel, means as ... as: mor boeth ag, as hot as.
Nid yn unig sets up not only, and pairs with ond hefyd, but also, later in the sentence.
Two has separate genders: dau gi, two dogs, but dwy gath, two cats. Both soft-mutate the noun after them.
Rhaid i plus a subject means must: Rhaid i'r traethawd fod, the dissertation must be. Welsh frames obligation as necessity.
